o: Every word has distinct lowercase letters, so each word is really a set of at most 26 letters. Two sets are connected if one edit bridges them: adding a letter, deleting a letter, or replacing one letter (possibly by itself). Connectivity is transitive and the induced partition into groups is unique; we report the number of groups and the largest group size. In Example 1 the sets {a}, {b} and {a,b} chain together — replacements link the singletons and additions attach ab — while {c,d,e} stands alone, giving [2,3]. Example 2 shows the chain a ⊂ ab ⊂ abc forming one group of size 3. With up to 2*10^4 words, comparing all ~2*10^8 pairs is borderline; encoding sets as 26-bit masks makes each comparison cheap and enables generating neighbors instead of scanning pairs.
k: A word with pairwise-distinct letters is exactly its letter set, faithfully encoded as a 26-bit bitmask.
One edit = XOR with a single bit (add/delete), or clear a set bit and set an unset bit (replace); replacing a letter with itself connects duplicate masks.
Generating each word's at most ~200 candidate neighbor masks and probing a hash map finds all edges in near-linear time, far beating pairwise comparison.

a.i: Compare 26-bit letter-set masks for every pair. Let d = mask_i XOR mask_j and pc = popcount(d): pc = 0 means identical sets (replace with itself), pc = 1 is an add or delete, and pc = 2 with equal mask popcounts is a replacement. Union every connected pair; the transitive closure yields the groups.
s: Encode each word as a 26-bit mask of its letters.
For every pair, compute d = mask_i XOR mask_j and pc = popcount(d).
Union the pair when pc == 0, pc == 1, or pc == 2 with equal mask popcounts.
Report the number of DSU roots and the largest component size.
a.t: O(n^2) — every pair tested once with O(1) bit arithmetic
a.sp: O(n) — masks plus the DSU parent array

a.i: Rather than testing all pairs, exploit how constrained one edit is. Flipping any of the 26 bits generates every add/delete neighbor; clearing one set bit and setting one unset bit generates at most |S|*(26-|S|) <= 169 replace neighbors. Keeping a hash map from mask to the first word that had it, each new word unions with whichever of its ~200 candidate masks were already seen — symmetry guarantees no edge is missed — while Union-Find maintains components.
s: Encode each word as a 26-bit mask; keep a map mask -> first word index seen with it.
Handle duplicates: union with the entry of the identical mask (replace with itself), then register the mask.
Probe all 26 one-bit flips (covers add and delete) and union on hits.
Probe all clear-one-bit/set-one-bit variants (covers replace) and union on hits.
Answer = number of DSU roots and the maximum component size.
a.t: O(n * 26^2) — each word probes at most 26 flip masks plus at most 169 replace masks
a.sp: O(n) — the mask hash map plus DSU arrays

w: Present the mask + neighbor-generation DSU as the main plan and cite the pairwise baseline only to motivate it. Pitfalls: treating replace-with-itself as a no-op (it is what links duplicate masks), missing that add and delete are both captured by flipping any of the 26 bits, and forgetting unconnected words form singleton groups. Follow-ups: alphabets beyond 26 letters (hash the multiset), dynamically inserting words, or materializing the actual groups by storing members per root.
